platforms.title: Bone Loss Isn't Just About Age - These Two Everyday Drinks Speed It Up
platforms.meta_description: Bone loss isn't only about getting older. Phosphoric acid in soda and daily caffeine both pull calcium from your body — here's what the research shows.
platforms.body_html:
It's easy to chalk up thinning bones to getting older, but two everyday habits — a can of soda and a daily coffee routine — are doing more to speed up calcium loss than most people realize. Neither one needs to disappear from your routine completely, but understanding how each one actually affects your bones makes it much easier to know where to focus.

It's Not Just Age: How Soda Pulls Calcium From Your Bones

Cola contains phosphoric acid, the ingredient behind its sharp, tangy taste. When phosphate levels in the blood rise, the body works to keep its calcium-to-phosphorus ratio balanced, and one way it does that is by pulling calcium out of bone. A widely cited analysis of the Framingham Osteoporosis Study, led by researchers at Tufts University, found that women who drank cola daily had hip bone density measurements roughly 2 to 5 percent lower than women who rarely drank it — a gap that didn't show up with other carbonated drinks without cola's phosphoric acid.

Coffee's Role Is Real, But Smaller Than Most People Assume

Caffeine increases how much calcium the body releases into urine for a few hours after each cup, and it can also interfere with calcium absorption in the gut. That sounds alarming, but the National Osteoporosis Foundation's actual guidance is fairly moderate: keeping caffeinated coffee or tea to three cups a day or fewer is generally enough to avoid meaningfully affecting calcium absorption. The bigger risk shows up in people who are already falling short on calcium and drinking well beyond that amount — it's the combination of the two that compounds the problem.

What Actually Helps

  • Get enough calcium daily — the Institute of Medicine recommends 1,000 mg a day for most adults under 50, rising to 1,200 mg for women 51 and older and men 71 and older. Dairy, calcium-fortified orange juice, and canned salmon with the bones still in are all easy ways to hit that number.
  • Keep soda to an occasional treat, and reach for sparkling water when you want something cold and fizzy instead.
  • Cap coffee around three cups a day, and pair it with a calcium source rather than cutting it out completely.
  • Weight-bearing exercise like walking or light strength training helps bones hold onto the calcium they already have.

The Bottom Line

Neither soda nor coffee needs to be eliminated to protect your bones — moderation and making sure calcium intake stays adequate matter more than cutting either one out completely. This article is for general information only and isn't medical advice; anyone concerned about bone density should talk to a doctor about a bone density scan.
